newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary mkt sees rate cut, some analysts doubtful.
newsitem.headline: Hungary mkt sees rate cut, some analysts doubtful.

text.p: Hungary's government securities markets expect the central bank to cut its benchmark one-year bond yield next week, which would be seen as a seal of approval on a sharp decline in market yields, analysts said on Friday.
But some analysts doubted the National Bank of Hungary would consent to the interest rate fall.
Attila Torok of Postabank Securities said interest rate levels, mainly the yields on six-month and 12-month Treasury bills, have declined too quickly for the National Bank of Hungary (NBH).
"In my opinion, the NBH does not think a sober thing for yields to fall so quickly," Torok said.
Government securities yields have been falling for two weeks, encouraged partly by a 0.5-percent repo rate cut on June 13 and abolition of the NBH's six- and 12-month deposit facilities last week.

On Tuesday rates fell further after Hungary said it would cut its 1.1-percent monthly crawling peg devaluation rate to one percent on August 15 and rating agency IBCA said it upgraded Hungary to BBB from BBB minus, analysts said.

Secondary market government securities yields have shed tens of basis points in the past two weeks, and yields on six- and 12-month Treasury bills fell at an unusually high rate on Thursday and Friday, they noted.
The six-month yield fell to 19.71 percent from 20.26 percent.
The 12-month yield was set at 19.77 percent, down from 20.18 percent, well below 20.27 percent, the current yield on the NBH's one-year bond.

"I have heard that the paper (the NBH bond) is bought in a very heavy volume," Pozsgay said, adding that the NBH may run out of the 75 billion forint ($401.6 million) worth of bonds and will have to issue new bonds or cut the yield.
Torok said investors who bought 12-month T-bills at 19.77 percent with a payment date on next Friday, were likely to lose as the NBH would probably not cut the yield on its bond.

He referred to an NBH statement released following Friday's 12-month T-bill yield auction, which said that the NBH would continue a cautious interest rate policy and that it was not satisfied with the level of household savings.

Torok said the situation was similar to that in early March, when a rapid interest rate decline followed the announcement of a 10 basis point cut in the devaluation rate and the NBH raised its six-month deposit rate and launched a 12-month deposit facility to protect savings.
